name: Disposition effect
statement: Investors sell shares that have risen since purchase at a higher rate than shares that have fallen, and the gap survives in tax years where the opposite would pay.
meaning: The claim is about rates, not counts. An investor holding twenty rising stocks and two falling ones will sell more winners than losers whatever their preferences, so the measure has to condition on opportunity. Odean's version divides realised gains by realised plus unrealised gains, and realised losses by realised plus unrealised losses. The two proportions are then compared. A ratio above one says that a position in profit is more likely to be closed on a given day than a position at a loss of the same age. Three quantities in this literature look alike and are not the same: the proportion of gains realised, the proportion of losses realised, and the gap between them. A paper reporting one of them has not reported the others. Three claims are also often run together under the one name. The first is the trading pattern itself, which is a fact about records. The second is that the pattern costs money, which needs a return comparison. The third is that prospect theory explains it, which is a claim about mechanism and is the weakest of the three.

origin.note: "The Disposition to Sell Winners Too Early and Ride Losers Too Long: Theory and Evidence" supplied the name. Its own contribution is a framework rather than a dataset. Only the abstract could be read for this check, and it starts from Kahneman and Tversky's aversion to loss realisation. Around that it sets four elements: mental accounting, which entry 182 covers, regret aversion, self-control and tax considerations. Tax considerations sit inside the framework rather than outside it, which is easy to misreport. Shefrin and Statman argue that tax considerations alone cannot explain the observed patterns of loss and gain realisation. They also argue that the concentration of loss realisations in December is inconsistent with fully rational behaviour. The measurement that made the claim testable on trading records came thirteen years later, from Odean.

evidence: Odean obtained the 1987 to 1993 trading records of 10,000 accounts at a large discount brokerage. Of those accounts, 6,380 traded stocks carried in the CRSP file, for 97,483 transactions, and that is the sample analysed. Aggregated over the whole period, the proportion of gains realised was 0.148 and the proportion of losses realised 0.098. Odean puts the ratio of the two at a little over 1.5. The one-tailed test that gains are realised no faster than losses is rejected with a t-statistic above 35. Odean also ran the test at account level rather than trade level, which weakens the independence assumption. Average account PGR was 0.57, average PLR 0.36, and the mean difference of 0.21 gives t = 19. December runs the other way. In December the proportion of losses realised was 0.128 against a proportion of gains realised of 0.108, and from January to November the figures were 0.094 and 0.152. Tax selling appears, and only in the last month. Grinblatt and Keloharju repeated the question on the Finnish Central Securities Depository register, the official daily record of holdings and trades of virtually all Finnish investors from 27 December 1994 to 10 January 1997. Their logit of sell against hold carries 244 regressors. Among them are 87 stock dummies, 25 month dummies and 22 past-return variables covering 11 horizons, entered separately for positive and negative returns. For households, on 122,765 observations, an extreme capital loss of more than 30 percent makes a sale 0.32 less likely than a capital gain at a predicted logit of zero, and a moderate loss 0.21 less likely. The equivalent OLS figures are 0.17 and 0.12.

examples.text: A small investor holds twelve shares. Of the four standing at a profit, three are sold within the year; of the five standing at a loss, none are. Counting the sales alone says little, and the rates are what make the pattern.

examples.tag: Waiting for it to come back
examples.text: A holder of a share well below what they paid says they will sell once it returns to that price, and sells a different holding the week it moves into profit. No new money is being spent on either, so nothing here is about protecting an outlay.

A landlord with one flat worth more than they paid and one worth less sells the first and keeps the second, though the tax position that year would favour the opposite. What sets the choice is which side of the purchase price each sits on.

replication.headline: The pattern reappears in the near-complete register of Finnish share ownership, in a second US brokerage sample and in retail records from several other markets, which is a stronger record than most entries on this site can show.
replication.detail: What distinguishes this case is the kind of repeat available. Most of the corpus is replicated by running an experiment again on fresh volunteers. Here the tests run on the administrative record of what people actually did with their own money, in different countries, under different tax codes, with sample sizes in the tens of thousands and no experimenter present. That removes demand characteristics, hypothetical stakes and small student samples in one move, which is why the pattern itself is close to settled. Grinblatt and Keloharju's Finnish register covers virtually every domestic investor rather than a sample of one broker's clients, and their controls include the stock, the month and the shape of past returns. The raw distributions in the same paper show the effect without controls: the density of realised returns drops sharply just to the left of zero, while the density of paper returns is smooth across zero. Chang, Solomon and Westerfield used 128,829 accounts at a large discount broker from January 1991 to November 1996, comprising 73,558 households drawn from 78,000 sampled, and estimated selling as a regression on a gain dummy. For stocks the coefficient runs from 0.0391 across all investors to 0.0157 among investors who hold both stocks and funds, against a base probability of selling of 21.7 and 18.9 percent. Those figures come from their April 2014 working paper, which is the version this check could open, and not from the 2016 article. Odean has also repeated his own measurement. In Barber and Odean's review, a hazard model on the discount-broker records for 1991 to 1996 makes a stock up 18 to 22 percent since purchase 2.65 times more likely to be sold than one within two percent of its purchase price, and 1.77 times more likely than one down 18 to 22 percent. They report Finnish data from 1995 to 2008 with a similar shape. From the same review: Chinese investors in one brokerage were 67 percent more likely to sell a winner than a loser across almost 50,000 accounts, Taiwanese individual investors nearly four times as likely, and US mutual funds realised gains at a rate 21 percent above losses from 1980 to 2002, rising to 72 percent for funds in the previous year's worst-performing quintile. Feng and Seasholes report in their abstract that sophistication and trading experience together remove the reluctance to realise losses while cutting the propensity to realise gains by 37 percent without removing it. Barber and Odean put that study at 1,511 Chinese investors who were 32 percent less likely to realise a loss. Weber and Camerer's laboratory version, as described by Barber and Odean, had subjects sell winners at a 50 percent higher rate than losers, with 60 percent of sales being winners. Cheung's meta-analysis of the experimental literature reports in its abstract that investors are around 10 percent more willing to sell winning than losing assets under baseline conditions.

study.cite: Grinblatt, M., & Keloharju, M. (2001). What makes investors trade? The Journal of Finance, 56(2), 589-616.

limits: Replication of a pattern is not replication of an explanation, and the two have come apart here. Ben-David and Hirshleifer went back to discount-broker records covering 77,037 accounts from 1990 to 1996 and asked whether selling jumps at exactly zero profit, which is what a preference for realising gains rather than losses predicts. It mostly does not. The probability of selling is V-shaped in profit, rising with the size of a gain and also with the size of a loss, and for positions held 1 to 20 days the discontinuity at zero is never significant and runs from about zero to 0.6 percent of the unconditional probability of selling. Pooled across all holding periods the jump reaches 4.1 to 5.7 percent, which they call economically minor. Those figures are from their December 2011 working paper, because the 2012 journal version could not be opened. Barberis and Xiong report in the abstract of the published article that prospect theory preferences defined over annual gains and losses often fail to predict a disposition effect at all, and that a version defined over realised gains and losses predicts it more reliably. Their 2006 working paper under the same title reaches only the first half of that, and its abstract carries no realised gain and loss model. None of these studies randomises anything. They compare investors who happen to be sitting on gains with investors sitting on losses, so beliefs, tax position, margin calls and rebalancing are controlled statistically rather than by design. The samples are also not populations. Odean's and Ben-David and Hirshleifer's are the clients of one discount broker, and the Finnish register drops foreign investors, who can register under a nominee, along with any holding whose purchase price falls outside the window. Cheung's meta-analysis of experimental disposition-effect studies could be read only in abstract. On 21 September 2026 SSRN answered with a Cloudflare bot challenge, the University of Sydney repository with a plain 403, and the working-paper host econ-wpseries.com had become a parked domain holding no files. None of those is a paywall, and no figure from the meta-analysis beyond the baseline above appears here. Searches of Crossref, OpenAlex and the web found no multi-site preregistered replication of the kind this site usually reports, which is unsurprising given that the evidence is archival rather than experimental.
misreadings: The commonest error is treating the effect as a demonstration of loss aversion. It is not the same claim. Loss aversion is a ratio between the weights on gains and losses of equal size, and entry 31 records how unstable that ratio is. The disposition effect is a fact about when positions are closed, and it survives whatever happens to lambda. Gal and Rucker, quoted in entry 31, put it in the class of findings that cannot speak to the ratio at all. It is also not the sunk-cost effect. Holding a losing share commits no new money, while the cases in entry 1 turn on spending more because of what was already spent. A second error is assuming investors are right about the rebound. Odean measured returns after the decision, in excess of the CRSP value-weighted index. Over the following 252 trading days the winners that were sold returned 2.35 percent and the losers that were held minus 1.06 percent, a gap of 3.41 percent with a bootstrapped p-value of 0.001. Over 84 days the gap is 1.03 percent and over 504 days 3.58 percent. A third error is calling the effect universal. Odean's own December figures reverse it. Chang, Solomon and Westerfield found the reverse in the same accounts for delegated assets: the gain coefficient for equity mutual funds runs from minus 0.0656 to minus 0.0485, so investors were 4.85 to 6.56 percent less likely to sell a fund standing at a gain. The base probability of selling a fund was 32.5 percent across all investors and 23.2 percent among those holding both. They trace the whole difference between stocks and funds to how readily a position at a loss is sold, not one at a gain. Whatever produces the pattern in stocks does not travel to money handed to someone else. The last error is reading the strength of the replication record as support for the prospect-theory story that gave the effect its name. The trading pattern is well established. The reason for it is not.

Abstract read at Crossref on 21 September 2026. Weber, M., & Camerer, C. F. (1998). The disposition effect in securities trading: An experimental analysis. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 33(2), 167-184. Record verified at Crossref, which holds no abstract for it. The Caltech and Mannheim repository records are metadata-only and hold no file, and ScienceDirect returned a bot challenge, so the paper was not read. The account given above is Barber and Odean's.
